### GRI 302 Energy  
Amazon reported 131,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of annual carbon-free energy production in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. Carbon-free energy includes electricity from wind, solar, nuclear, hydroelectric, and geothermal sources, as well as site energy contracts and green tariffs that add new renewable projects to the grid [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_14]. As of January 2026, Amazon’s renewable energy portfolio comprised 375 utility-scale projects globally—264 solar, 109 wind, and two nuclear—across 30 U.S. states and 15 European countries, with a total expected capacity of 41,670 MW [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_114][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. In 2025, emissions from purchased electricity (Scope 2) totaled 3.74 million metric tons of CO₂e (MMTCO₂e), representing a 34% increase from 2024 and 5% of Amazon’s total carbon footprint [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_19]. This growth was driven by increased electricity use in data centers, electrification of the delivery network, and building electrification [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_19].

### GRI 303 Water  
Amazon achieved 75% progress toward its goal of becoming water positive across global direct data center operations by 2030 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. In 2025, Amazon’s leased, owned, and shared data centers withdrew 9.4 billion liters of water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. The company’s global Water Use Effectiveness (WUE) improved to 0.12 liters per kilowatt-hour (L/kWh) —a 20% improvement from 2024 and 52% since 2021—driven by innovations including Direct Evaporative Cooling (used <10% of the year), In-Row Heat Exchangers (IRHX), and smart-metering technology that reduced global cooling water use by 938 million liters [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_35]. In India—where Amazon achieved 120% water positivity in 2025—on-site sewage treatment plants at 28 buildings provided an estimated 298 million liters of recycled water annually for non-potable uses, and rainwater harvesting pits collected ~178 million liters [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37]. Amazon also invested in 45 global water replenishment projects, which returned 9.4 billion liters to communities by end-2025 and are contracted to deliver over 18 billion liters annually once fully operational [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Amazon’s total carbon footprint (Scopes 1, 2, and 3) was 80.85 MMTCO₂e in 2025, up 16% from 69.55 MMTCO₂e in 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Scope 1 emissions were 15.37 MMTCO₂e; Scope 2, 3.74 MMTCO₂e; and Scope 3, 61.74 MMTCO₂e [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs) delivered a net reduction of 199.4 thousand metric tons of CO₂e (KMT CO₂e) across Scopes 1, 3.1, 3.3, and 3.4—including 41.2 KMT CO₂e reduction in Scope 1 via Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Renewable Diesel certificates [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_15][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_113]. Carbon intensity—measured as grams CO₂e per dollar of revenue—was 112.8 gCO₂e/$Revenue in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Amazon’s Climate Pledge commits to net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, supported by decarbonization, neutralization, and collective action [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112].

### GRI 306 Waste  
In 2025, Amazon diverted 84% of its operational waste from landfill and incineration without energy recovery—82% through recycling or composting and 2% via incineration with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Waste per shipped unit decreased by 5% compared to 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. Cardboard and wood constituted 64% of Amazon’s operational waste footprint, with nearly 100% recycled [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Across data centers, Amazon avoided over one million hard drive purchases since 2023 and prevented 225,000 metric tons of CO₂e through hardware reuse and resale since 2020 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. For Devices, 89 supplier sites achieved a verified 99% waste diversion rate in 2025, including 6% via thermal processing with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Amazon’s climate strategy is anchored in The Climate Pledge and structured around five pillars: supply chain decarbonization, direct operations decarbonization, emissions reduction from purchased electricity, carbon neutralization, and collective action [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Risk management integrates AI-driven supplier risk identification and Higg Facility Environmental Module (Higg FEM) assessments to prioritize audits and verify performance on carbon, waste, and water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_13][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Key metrics include carbon intensity (gCO₂e/$Revenue), WUE (L/kWh), and waste diversion rate (%), all tracked annually against 2040 net-zero, 2030 water-positive, and 2030 zero-waste-to-landfill targets [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45].

### Not covered in source material  
No information was found regarding: (1) location-based vs market-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown; (2) Scope 3 Category 11 (use of sold products) beyond device-related emissions; (3) detailed waste composition beyond cardboard/wood; (4) water withdrawal by source (e.g., surface, groundwater); (5) TCFD-aligned scenario analysis or physical climate risk assessment methodology; (6) assurance scope for water or waste data.

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Amazon’s global operations safety performance showed consistent improvement in 2025. The company reported a 14% year-over-year reduction in its Global Recordable Incident Rate (RIR), defined as any work-related injury requiring more than basic first-aid treatment, and a 14% year-over-year reduction in its Global Lost Time Incident Rate (LTIR), defined as any work-related injury requiring time away from work [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Over the prior six years, RIR improved by 43% and LTIR by 70% globally [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In the U.S., under the General Warehousing and Storage industry classification, RIR improved 16% year over year and 39% over six years; LTIR was flat year over year but improved 79% over six years [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Under the Courier and Express Delivery Services classification, RIR improved 19% year over year and 59% over six years, while LTIR improved 28% year over year and 81% over six years [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Amazon employed more than 11,000 safety professionals worldwide in 2025 and conducted 10.4 million global safety inspections—a 33% increase from 2024—to validate engineering controls and inform iterative improvements [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_77][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76].

### Training  
Amazon invested more than $2.5 billion in safety efforts since 2019, including training programs grounded in prevention-through-design principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In 2025, the company developed 52 new e-learning resources and updated 90 existing modules for employees on human rights topics, including forced labor risk identification, available in seven languages [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. It also piloted a three-day immersive training program for employees in human rights–related roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. For upskilling, Amazon launched the Automation Engineer Apprenticeship program—registered with the U.S. Department of Labor—and expanded its Mechatronics and Robotics Apprenticeship, through which graduates earned on average $10,000 more annually than typical entry-level fulfillment-center wages in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Since announcing its Upskilling Pledge in 2019, 599,000 U.S. employees participated in upskilling programs by 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_69].

### Diversity  
Amazon’s 2025 pay equity review found women globally earned 100.0% of what men earned in comparable jobs, and women in the U.S. earned 99.9 cents for every dollar earned by men in comparable roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Racial and ethnic minorities in the U.S. earned 99.0 cents for every dollar white employees earned in comparable jobs [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. The company reported that 647,000 corporate and operations employees engaged with the Together at Amazon Community in 2025, which includes 2,300 chapters of Employee-Led Groups (ELGs) across multiple countries and regions [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_75].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Amazon’s Supply Chain Standards—available in 23 languages—apply to all suppliers of goods and services, including subcontractors and recruitment agents, and require adherence to applicable laws and human rights standards [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_84][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_83]. In 2025, Amazon deployed online training to 1,600 suppliers on these standards and provided access to 90 third-party online trainings on 12 human rights topics, including fair wages and nondiscrimination [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_84]. It hosted 29 in-person human rights workshops across 13 countries, engaging 650 participants from 480 suppliers; 60% of suppliers attending workshops between 2023 and 2025 reduced high-risk audit findings [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_84]. Amazon requires suppliers to maintain effective worker grievance mechanisms and collaborates with them to develop such systems [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66].

### Supporting a Just Climate Transition  
Amazon aims to integrate human rights due diligence into its decarbonization efforts to identify how its green economy transition affects communities across its value chain [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66]. In 2025, it focused on carbon-free energy procurement, climate finance, and community-based carbon neutralization projects to align its net-zero commitment with human rights principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_67].

### Board Oversight and Committee Structure  
Amazon’s Board of Directors maintains formal oversight of enterprise-wide risks through four standing committees, each with defined governance mandates. The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee oversees risks related to sustainability, environmental and social responsibility, supply chain practices, and responsible AI development and governance [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. The Leadership Development and Compensation Committee oversees human capital management risks—including workplace health and safety, discrimination, harassment, diversity, and culture—as well as executive compensation and succession planning [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. The Audit Committee oversees financial reporting integrity, business continuity, operational risks, legal and regulatory compliance, tax matters, political contributions and lobbying expenses, and the performance of internal audit and independent auditors [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. The Security Committee oversees data protection, cybersecurity, physical security, and incident response, reporting annually to the Board and receiving regular updates from the Chief Security Officer [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. In 2025, the full Board held six in-person meetings and engaged in regularly scheduled teleconference discussions on governance topics [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_101]. Committee meeting frequencies in 2025 were: Nominating and Corporate Governance (four meetings), Leadership Development and Compensation (five meetings), Audit (six meetings), and Security (two meetings) [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102].

### Climate-Related and Human Rights Governance  
Climate-related governance is embedded within the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee’s mandate, which includes oversight of sustainability and environmental risk management across operations and the supply chain [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_103]. The Chief Sustainability Officer provides regular updates to this committee and oversees Amazon’s companywide carbon system of record, which tracks business-level emissions to support decarbonization progress [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104]. Human rights governance is coordinated through dual oversight: the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee monitors policies on corporate social responsibility and ethical business practices, while the Leadership Development and Compensation Committee oversees internal human capital policies, including nondiscrimination, workplace safety, and culture [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104]. Amazon employs a dedicated Human Rights Officer who reports directly to the Chief Sustainability Officer and facilitates regular risk management updates to senior leadership [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104].

### Anti-Corruption and Ethics Infrastructure  
Amazon’s anti-corruption program is led by the Vice President for Business Conduct and Ethics, who reports to the Senior Vice President, Chief Global Affairs & Legal Officer [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106]. The program includes a formal review process for allegations—investigated by the Business Conduct and Ethics team and reported to the Audit Committee—with disciplinary consequences up to termination [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106]. Employees are required to disclose and seek approval for gifts or entertainment involving government officials, and mechanisms exist for conflict-of-interest disclosure and remediation [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107]. Third-party due diligence follows a risk-based approach prior to engagement [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107]. All employees receive Code of Conduct training during onboarding and periodic refreshers; leadership and the Board receive specialized training on anti-corruption and competition law [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107]. Amazon participates in the OECD’s Anti-Corruption Leaders Hub to advance digitized compliance and partner vetting initiatives [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107].

### Ethics Reporting and Accountability Mechanisms  
Amazon operates a confidential, third-party-managed Ethics Line available in 65 countries and 165 languages, enabling anonymous reporting of Code violations and ethical concerns [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106]. Additional secure channels include Human Resources, the Legal Department, and any manager [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106]. The Business Conduct and Ethics team records, investigates, and tracks remediation of reported issues, with findings escalated to the Audit Committee [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106]. Senior leadership receives regular updates on harassment and discrimination allegations involving director-level personnel; the Leadership Development and Compensation Committee receives detailed quarterly updates for vice-president-level and above cases or those subject to external investigation [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106].

### GRI 302 Energy  
Amazon reported 131,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of annual carbon-free energy production in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. Carbon-free energy includes electricity generated from wind, solar, nuclear, hydroelectric, and geothermal sources, as well as site energy contracts and green tariffs that add new renewable projects to the grid [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_14]. As of January 2026, Amazon’s renewable energy portfolio comprised 375 utility-scale projects globally—264 solar, 109 wind, and two nuclear—with a total expected capacity of 41,670 MW across 30 U.S. states and 15 European countries [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_114][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. Emissions from purchased electricity (Scope 2) totaled 3.74 million metric tons of CO₂e (MMTCO₂e) in 2025, representing a 34% increase from 2024 and 5% of Amazon’s total carbon footprint [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_19]. This growth was driven by electricity use in data centers, electrification of the delivery network, and building electrification [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_19]. **The context does not disclose location-based or market-based Scope 2 emissions separately, nor does it specify whether the 131,000 GWh refers to physical generation or contracted renewable energy attributes** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22].

### GRI 303 Water  
Amazon aims to be water positive—returning more water to communities than it uses—across global direct data center operations by 2030 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. The target baseline year is not specified in the context; the absolute volume target (e.g., liters replenished annually) is also not disclosed [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. In 2025, Amazon’s leased, owned, and shared data centers withdrew 9.4 billion liters of water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. The company achieved 75% progress toward its 2030 data center water positive goal, up from 53% in 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. Global Water Use Effectiveness (WUE) improved to 0.12 liters per kilowatt-hour (L/kWh) in 2025—a 20% improvement from 0.15 L/kWh in 2024 and a 52% improvement from 0.25 L/kWh in 2021 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_35]. In India, Amazon achieved 120% water positivity in 2025—two years ahead of its 2027 goal—through on-site sewage treatment plants (28 buildings, yielding ~298 million liters/year), rainwater harvesting (~178 million liters infiltrated in 2025), and expanded replenishment investments [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37]. Amazon invested in 45 global water replenishment projects, returning 9.4 billion liters to communities by end-2025 and contracting for over 18 billion liters of annual replenishment volume in future years [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37]. **The context does not specify water withdrawal by source (e.g., surface water, groundwater, municipal supply) or identify root causes for the remaining gap to full water positivity (e.g., regulatory constraints, infrastructure limitations)** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_34].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Amazon’s total carbon footprint (Scopes 1, 2, and 3) was 80.85 million metric tons of CO₂e (MMTCO₂e) in 2025, up 16% from 69.55 MMTCO₂e in 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Scope 1 emissions were 15.37 MMTCO₂e; Scope 2, 3.74 MMTCO₂e; and Scope 3, 61.74 MMTCO₂e [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs) delivered a net reduction of 199.4 thousand metric tons of CO₂e (KMT CO₂e) across Scopes 1, 3.1, 3.3, and 3.4—including 41.2 KMT CO₂e reduction in Scope 1 via Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Renewable Diesel certificates [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_15][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_113]. Carbon intensity—measured as grams CO₂e per dollar of revenue—was 112.8 gCO₂e/$Revenue in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. **The context discloses only partial Scope 3 category breakdowns: Scopes 3.1 (purchased goods and services), 3.3 (fuel- and energy-related activities), and 3.4 (downstream transportation and distribution) are quantified, but emissions for the remaining 12 GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories (e.g., Category 1 — upstream transportation, Category 11 — use of sold products beyond devices, Category 15 — investments) are not provided, nor is a GRI-compliant rationale for exclusions** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_113].

### GRI 306 Waste  
In 2025, Amazon diverted 84% of its operational waste from landfill and incineration without energy recovery—82% through recycling or composting and 2% via incineration with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Waste per shipped unit decreased by 5% compared to 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. Cardboard and wood constituted 64% of Amazon’s operational waste footprint, with nearly 100% recycled [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Across data centers, Amazon avoided over one million hard drive purchases since 2023 and prevented 225,000 metric tons of CO₂e through hardware reuse and resale since 2020 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. For Devices, 89 supplier sites achieved a verified 99% waste diversion rate in 2025, including 6% via thermal processing with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45]. **The context does not disclose waste composition beyond cardboard and wood, nor does it explain reasons for residual landfill disposal (e.g., contamination, local infrastructure limits), nor state whether waste data are assured** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Amazon’s climate strategy is anchored in The Climate Pledge and structured around five pillars: supply chain decarbonization, direct operations decarbonization, emissions reduction from purchased electricity, carbon neutralization, and collective action [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Risk management integrates AI-driven supplier risk identification and Higg Facility Environmental Module (Higg FEM) assessments to prioritize audits and verify performance on carbon, waste, and water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_13][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Key metrics include carbon intensity (gCO₂e/$Revenue), WUE (L/kWh), and waste diversion rate (%), all tracked annually against 2040 net-zero, 2030 water-positive, and 2030 zero-waste-to-landfill targets [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45]. **The context does not describe any TCFD-aligned scenario analysis—including assumptions, scenarios tested (e.g., 1.5°C, 2°C), or strategic implications—or disclose physical climate risk assessment methodology** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10].

### Not covered in source material  
No information was found regarding: (1) location-based vs market-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown (GRI 302-2); (2) Scope 3 emissions disaggregated by all 15 GHG Protocol categories or a GRI-compliant justification for omissions (GRI 305-2); (3) water withdrawal by source (e.g., surface, groundwater, municipal supply) (GRI 303-3); (4) detailed waste composition beyond cardboard/wood (GRI 306-2); (5) TCFD-aligned scenario analysis or physical climate risk assessment methodology (TCFD Metrics & Targets); (6) assurance status for water or waste data; (7) root causes of remaining water positivity gap (e.g., regional regulatory barriers, infrastructure deficits); (8) reasons for residual landfill waste (e.g., contamination rates, local recycling infrastructure limits); (9) baseline year or absolute volume target for water positivity (e.g., “X billion liters replenished annually by 2030”); (10) 2024 WUE value presented alongside the 20% YoY improvement claim (though 0.15 L/kWh is cited in [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_35], it is not explicitly tied to 2024 in the same sentence as the % change in [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]); (11) clarification of whether “131,000 GWh carbon-free energy production” refers to physical generation or contracted renewable energy attributes.

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Amazon’s 2025 Global Recordable Incident Rate (RIR) — defined as any work-related injury requiring more than basic first-aid treatment — improved 14% year over year; its Global Lost Time Incident Rate (LTIR) — defined as any work-related injury requiring time away from work — also improved 14% year over year [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Over the six-year period 2019–2025, RIR improved by 43% and LTIR by 70% globally [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In the U.S., under the General Warehousing and Storage industry classification, RIR improved 16% year over year (2024–2025) and 39% since 2019; LTIR was flat year over year but improved 79% since 2019 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Under the Courier and Express Delivery Services classification, RIR improved 19% year over year and 59% since 2019; LTIR improved 28% year over year and 81% since 2019 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Amazon employed more than 11,000 safety professionals worldwide in 2025 and conducted 10.4 million global safety inspections — a 33% increase from 2024 — to validate engineering controls and inform iterative improvements [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_77][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. The methodology for RIR and LTIR is not disclosed in the source material, nor are incident rates reported per 100,000 hours worked or by operating segment (e.g., AWS, International, Consumer). No baseline year, deadline, or science-aligned target (e.g., “<2.0 RIR by 2030”) is stated [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76].

### Training  
Amazon invested more than $2.5 billion in safety efforts since 2019, including training programs grounded in prevention-through-design principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In 2025, it developed 52 new e-learning resources and updated 90 existing modules on human rights topics — such as responsible recruitment and fair wages — available in seven languages for employees [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. It also piloted a three-day immersive training program for employees in human rights–related roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. For upskilling, Amazon launched the Automation Engineer Apprenticeship program — registered with the U.S. Department of Labor — and expanded its Mechatronics and Robotics Apprenticeship; graduates earned on average $10,000 more annually than typical entry-level fulfillment-center wages in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Since announcing its Upskilling Pledge in 2019, 599,000 U.S. employees participated in upskilling programs by 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_69]. The source does not disclose training completion rates, participation gaps by demographic group, or aggregate reach of human rights training across employee populations. No forward-looking target for training coverage or effectiveness is stated.

### Diversity  
Amazon’s 2025 pay equity review found women globally earned 100.0% of what men earned in comparable jobs, and women in the U.S. earned 99.9 cents for every dollar earned by men in comparable roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Racial and ethnic minorities in the U.S. earned 99.0 cents for every dollar white employees earned in comparable jobs [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. The company reported that 647,000 corporate and operations employees engaged with the Together at Amazon Community in 2025, which includes 2,300 chapters of Employee-Led Groups (ELGs) across multiple countries and regions [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_75]. However, no gender or racial/ethnic representation data is provided by job level (e.g., leadership, management, operational), geography (e.g., North America, EMEA, APAC), or disability/LGBTQ+ status — nor are targets for representation published. The source contains no disclosure of representation gaps, root-cause analysis of pay variances by level or region, or progress against prior-year diversity goals.

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Amazon’s Supply Chain Standards — available in 23 languages — apply to all suppliers of goods and services, including subcontractors and recruitment agents, and require adherence to applicable laws and human rights standards [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_84][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_83]. In 2025, Amazon conducted 3,081 supplier audits across its logistics, warehousing, and construction supply chain, including 1,579 audits focused on third-party labor, service, and not-for-resale goods providers [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_85]. Audit findings are categorized as high-, medium-, or low-severity; high-severity findings require corrective action plans and follow-up audits [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88]. However, the source does not disclose the total number or percentage of suppliers assessed, the number or rate of non-compliant suppliers, the proportion of high-risk findings unresolved after 90 days, or audit results disaggregated by tier (Tier 1–3) or geography. No supplier non-compliance rate or remediation timeline metric is reported.

### Supporting a Just Climate Transition  
Amazon states it aims to integrate human rights due diligence into its decarbonization efforts “so we can better identify how our shift to a green economy might affect the communities in our value chain” [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66]. In 2025, it focused on carbon-free energy procurement, climate finance, and community-based carbon neutralization projects to align its net-zero commitment with human rights principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_67]. However, the source contains no TCFD-aligned social impact assessment of Amazon’s net-zero pathway — including no analysis of projected workforce transitions, reskilling needs, community displacement risks, or equity safeguards for affected workers or regions. No baseline, target year, or measurable indicator is provided for human rights integration into climate strategy.

### Not covered in source material  
GRI 405-2 and 405-3: Gender and racial/ethnic representation by job level (e.g., senior leadership, management, operational staff) and major region (e.g., North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific); disability and LGBTQ+ representation metrics.  
GRI 414-3 and 414-4: Number and percentage of suppliers assessed, non-compliant suppliers, and remediation status — disaggregated by tier (Tier 1–3), geography, and severity level; supplier non-compliance rate; % of high-risk findings unresolved after 90 days.  
TCFD Strategy (social impacts of climate transition): TCFD-aligned social risk assessment of Amazon’s decarbonization pathways, including projected workforce transitions, reskilling gaps, community displacement or economic disruption risks, and equity-focused mitigation measures.  
Forward-looking targets: Science-aligned occupational health & safety target (e.g., RIR/LTIR reduction goal with baseline and deadline); representation targets by gender, race/ethnicity, and disability for senior leadership and board by 2030; measurable target for human rights due diligence integration (e.g., % of Tier 1 suppliers assessed for climate-transition social risks).  
Transparency on challenges: RIR/LTIR performance by operating segment; progress against prior-year targets, including missed goals and root-cause analysis; methodology for RIR/LTIR calculation (e.g., denominator, OSHA alignment); definition of “engaged” or “inspection” in context of safety metrics.

### Board Oversight and Committee Structure  
Amazon’s Board of Directors maintains formal oversight of enterprise-wide risks through four standing committees, each with defined governance mandates aligned with GRI 2-8 (governance structure) and TCFD Governance A1 (board oversight of climate-related risks) [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee oversees risks related to sustainability, environmental and social responsibility, supply chain practices, and responsible AI development and governance [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-8; TCFD Governance A1]. The Leadership Development and Compensation Committee oversees human capital management risks—including workplace health and safety, discrimination, harassment, diversity, and culture—as well as executive compensation and succession planning [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-8]. The Audit Committee oversees financial reporting integrity, business continuity, operational risks, legal and regulatory compliance, tax matters, political contributions and lobbying expenses, and the performance of internal audit and independent auditors [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-8]. The Security Committee oversees data protection, cybersecurity, physical security, and incident response, reporting annually to the Board and receiving regular updates from the Chief Security Officer [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-8]. In 2025, the full Board held six in-person meetings and engaged in regularly scheduled teleconference discussions on governance topics [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_101][GRI 2-8]. Committee meeting frequencies in 2025 were: Nominating and Corporate Governance (four meetings), Leadership Development and Compensation (five meetings), Audit (six meetings), and Security (two meetings) [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-8]. No comparative data for 2024 committee or Board meeting frequencies is provided in the source material.

### Board Diversity Composition  
The source material states that the Board’s composition is evaluated for “diversity of experiences, backgrounds, and perspectives” and that recruitment considers “skills in the context of identifying and evaluating new director candidates,” but it does not disclose quantitative board diversity metrics—including percentage of women directors, representation of underrepresented ethnicities, or average director tenure—as required by GRI 2-11 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][GRI 2-11]. No numerical or categorical breakdown of director demographics is included in the retrieved context.

### Board Oversight of Climate Risk  
The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee is explicitly responsible for overseeing climate-related risks as part of its mandate for sustainability and environmental risk management [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_103][TCFD Governance A1]. The Chief Sustainability Officer provides “regular updates” to this committee on sustainability performance, including climate-related matters [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104][TCFD Governance A1]. However, the source material does not specify the frequency (e.g., quarterly, biannual), format (e.g., written reports, presentations), or analytical methodology (e.g., scenario analysis, physical risk mapping) used in these updates [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104]. Nor does it disclose whether dedicated climate risk reviews occur at the full Board level or across other committees beyond the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee. No TCFD-aligned target for board-level climate risk assessment maturity—such as adoption of annual climate risk deep-dives across all committees—is stated in the context [TCFD Governance A1].

### Management Oversight of Climate Risk  
Amazon’s Sustainability team coordinates operational decarbonization efforts and maintains a “companywide carbon system of record” that provides business-level emissions information to track progress [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104][TCFD Risk Management A2]. The Sustainability team reports to senior leadership quarterly on environmental and sustainability practices, and senior leadership holds quarterly business reviews with business units to track progress against The Climate Pledge commitments [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104][TCFD Risk Management A2]. No further detail on management-level climate risk identification, prioritization, or integration into strategic planning is provided.

### Anti-Corruption and Ethics Infrastructure  
Amazon’s anti-corruption program is led by the Vice President for Business Conduct and Ethics, who reports to the Senior Vice President, Chief Global Affairs & Legal Officer [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. The program includes a formal review process for allegations—investigated by the Business Conduct and Ethics team and reported to the Audit Committee—with disciplinary consequences up to termination [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. Employees are required to disclose and seek approval for gifts or entertainment involving government officials, and mechanisms exist for conflict-of-interest disclosure and remediation [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107][GRI 205-1]. Third-party due diligence follows a “risk-based approach,” but the source material does not define criteria for classifying third parties as high-risk, nor does it quantify the scope or coverage of due diligence activities [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107][GRI 205-1]. All employees receive Code of Conduct training during onboarding and periodic refreshers; leadership and the Board receive specialized training on anti-corruption and competition law [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107][GRI 205-1]. The source material does not state the mandated interval for refresher training [GRI 205-1].

### Ethics Reporting and Accountability Mechanisms  
Amazon operates a confidential, third-party-managed Ethics Line available in 65 countries and 165 languages, enabling anonymous reporting of Code violations and ethical concerns [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. Additional secure channels include Human Resources, the Legal Department, and any manager [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. The Business Conduct and Ethics team records, investigates, and tracks remediation of reported issues, with findings escalated to the Audit Committee [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. Senior leadership receives regular updates on harassment and discrimination allegations involving director-level personnel; the Leadership Development and Compensation Committee receives detailed quarterly updates for vice-president-level and above cases or those subject to external investigation [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. However, the source material does not disclose the total number of Ethics Line reports received in 2025, the number of substantiated corruption allegations, the number of investigations opened or closed, disciplinary actions taken, average or median resolution time, or any instances where investigations exceeded 90-day resolution targets [GRI 205-1]. No 2024 baseline or trend comparison is provided [GRI 205-1].

### GRI 302 Energy  
Amazon reported 131,000 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of annual carbon-free energy production in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. Carbon-free energy includes electricity generated from wind, solar, nuclear, hydroelectric, and geothermal sources, as well as site energy contracts and green tariffs that add new renewable projects to the grid [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_14]. As of January 2026, Amazon’s renewable energy portfolio comprised 375 utility-scale projects globally—264 solar, 109 wind, and two nuclear—with a total expected capacity of 41,670 MW across 30 U.S. states and 15 European countries [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_114][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22]. Emissions from purchased electricity (Scope 2) totaled 3.74 million metric tons of CO₂e (MMTCO₂e) in 2025, representing 4.6% of Amazon’s total carbon footprint of 80.85 MMTCO₂e [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. This growth was driven by electricity use in data centers, electrification of the delivery network, and building electrification [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_19]. **The context does not disclose location-based or market-based Scope 2 emissions separately, nor does it specify whether the 131,000 GWh refers to physical generation, contractual procurement of renewable energy attributes, or a hybrid** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_22].

### GRI 303 Water  
Amazon aims to be water positive—returning more water to communities than it uses—across global direct data center operations by 2030 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. The baseline year for this target is not disclosed in the context, nor is an absolute volume target (e.g., liters replenished annually) specified [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. In 2025, Amazon’s leased, owned, and shared data centers withdrew 9.4 billion liters of water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. The company achieved 75% progress toward its 2030 data center water positive goal, up from 53% in 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33]. Global Water Use Effectiveness (WUE) improved to 0.12 liters per kilowatt-hour (L/kWh) in 2025—a 20% reduction from 0.15 L/kWh in 2024 and a 52% reduction from 0.25 L/kWh in 2021 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_35]. In India, Amazon achieved 120% water positivity in 2025—two years ahead of its 2027 goal—through on-site sewage treatment plants (28 buildings, yielding ~298 million liters/year), rainwater harvesting (~178 million liters infiltrated in 2025), and expanded replenishment investments [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37]. Amazon invested in 45 global water replenishment projects, returning 9.4 billion liters to communities by end-2025 and contracting for over 18 billion liters of annual replenishment volume in future years [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_37]. **The context does not specify water withdrawal by source (e.g., surface water, groundwater, municipal supply) or identify root causes for the remaining gap to full water positivity** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_34].

### GRI 305 Emissions  
Amazon’s total carbon footprint (Scopes 1, 2, and 3) was 80.85 million metric tons of CO₂e (MMTCO₂e) in 2025, up 16% from 69.55 MMTCO₂e in 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Scope 1 emissions were 15.37 MMTCO₂e; Scope 2, 3.74 MMTCO₂e; and Scope 3, 61.74 MMTCO₂e [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. Environmental Attribute Certificates (EACs) delivered a net reduction of 199.4 thousand metric tons of CO₂e (KMT CO₂e) across Scopes 1, 3.1, 3.3, and 3.4—including 41.2 KMT CO₂e reduction in Scope 1 via Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and Renewable Diesel certificates [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_15][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_113]. Carbon intensity—measured as grams CO₂e per dollar of revenue—was 112.8 gCO₂e/$Revenue in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112]. **The context discloses only partial Scope 3 category breakdowns: Scopes 3.1 (purchased goods and services), 3.3 (fuel- and energy-related activities), and 3.4 (downstream transportation and distribution) are quantified, but emissions for the remaining 12 GHG Protocol Scope 3 categories (e.g., Category 1 — upstream transportation, Category 11 — use of sold products beyond devices, Category 15 — investments) are not provided, nor is a GRI-compliant rationale for exclusions** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_112][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_113].

### GRI 306 Waste  
In 2025, Amazon diverted 84% of its operational waste from landfill and incineration without energy recovery—82% through recycling or composting and 2% via incineration with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Waste per shipped unit decreased by 5% compared to 2024 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. Cardboard and wood constituted 64% of Amazon’s operational waste footprint, with nearly 100% recycled [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47]. Across data centers, Amazon avoided over one million hard drive purchases since 2023 and prevented 225,000 metric tons of CO₂e through hardware reuse and resale since 2020 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_41]. For Devices, 89 supplier sites achieved a verified 99% waste diversion rate in 2025, including 6% via thermal processing with energy recovery [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45]. **The context does not disclose waste composition beyond cardboard and wood, nor does it explain reasons for residual landfill disposal (e.g., contamination, local infrastructure limits), nor state whether waste data are assured** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_47][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45].

### TCFD Strategy, Risk Management, Metrics & Targets  
Amazon’s climate strategy is anchored in The Climate Pledge and structured around five pillars: supply chain decarbonization, direct operations decarbonization, emissions reduction from purchased electricity, carbon neutralization, and collective action [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Risk management integrates AI-driven supplier risk identification and Higg Facility Environmental Module (Higg FEM) assessments to prioritize audits and verify performance on carbon, waste, and water [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_13][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10]. Key metrics include carbon intensity (gCO₂e/$Revenue), WUE (L/kWh), and waste diversion rate (%), all tracked annually against 2040 net-zero, 2030 water-positive, and 2030 zero-waste-to-landfill targets [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_5][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_33][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_45]. **The context does not describe any TCFD-aligned scenario analysis—including assumptions, scenarios tested (e.g., 1.5°C, 2°C), or strategic implications—or disclose physical climate risk assessment methodology** [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_10].

### Not covered in source material  
No information was found regarding: (1) location-based vs market-based Scope 2 emissions breakdown (GRI 302-2); (2) Scope 3 emissions disaggregated by all 15 GHG Protocol categories or a GRI-compliant justification for omissions (GRI 305-2); (3) water withdrawal by source (e.g., surface, groundwater, municipal supply) (GRI 303-3); (4) detailed waste composition beyond cardboard/wood (GRI 306-2); (5) TCFD-aligned scenario analysis or physical climate risk assessment methodology (TCFD Metrics & Targets); (6) assurance status for water or waste data (GRI 102-32, GRI 102-33); (7) baseline year or absolute volume target for the 2030 water positivity goal (GRI 303-2); (8) baseline year and absolute % or tonnage target for the zero-waste-to-landfill goal (GRI 306-2); (9) interim milestones or 2025 baseline for the 2040 net-zero target (TCFD Metrics & Targets); (10) clarification of whether “131,000 GWh carbon-free energy production” refers to physical generation, contractual procurement, or a hybrid (GRI 302-1); (11) root causes of remaining water positivity gap (e.g., regional regulatory barriers, infrastructure deficits); (12) reasons for residual landfill waste (e.g., contamination rates, local recycling infrastructure limits).

### Occupational Health & Safety  
Amazon’s 2025 Global Recordable Incident Rate (RIR) improved 14% year over year; its Global Lost Time Incident Rate (LTIR) also improved 14% year over year [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Over the six-year period 2019–2025, RIR improved by 43% and LTIR by 70% globally [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In the U.S., under the General Warehousing and Storage industry classification, RIR improved 16% year over year (2024–2025) and 39% since 2019; LTIR was flat year over year but improved 79% since 2019 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Under the Courier and Express Delivery Services classification, RIR improved 19% year over year and 59% since 2019; LTIR improved 28% year over year and 81% since 2019 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. Amazon employed more than 11,000 safety professionals worldwide in 2025 and conducted 10.4 million global safety inspections — a 33% increase from 2024 — to validate engineering controls and inform iterative improvements [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_77][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. The source does not disclose absolute RIR or LTIR values for 2019, 2024, or 2025, nor does it specify the denominator (e.g., hours worked), normalization basis (e.g., per 100,000 hours), or OSHA alignment of definitions [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76]. No science-aligned, time-bound target (e.g., “RIR ≤ 2.0 by 2030”) is stated, and no explanation is provided for why U.S. LTIR was flat year over year despite concurrent RIR improvement [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_76].

### Training  
Amazon invested more than $2.5 billion in safety efforts since 2019, including training programs grounded in prevention-through-design principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_78]. In 2025, it developed 52 new e-learning resources and updated 90 existing modules on human rights topics — such as responsible recruitment and fair wages — available in seven languages for employees [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. It also piloted a three-day immersive training program for employees in human rights–related roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63]. For upskilling, Amazon launched the Automation Engineer Apprenticeship program — registered with the U.S. Department of Labor — and expanded its Mechatronics and Robotics Apprenticeship; graduates earned on average $10,000 more annually than typical entry-level fulfillment-center wages in 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Since announcing its Upskilling Pledge in 2019, 599,000 U.S. employees participated in upskilling programs by 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_69]. The source does not disclose training completion rates, participation gaps by demographic group, aggregate reach of human rights training across employee populations, or forward-looking targets for training coverage or effectiveness [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_63][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_69].

### Diversity  
Amazon’s 2025 pay equity review found women globally earned 100.0% of what men earned in comparable jobs, and women in the U.S. earned 99.9 cents for every dollar earned by men in comparable roles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. Racial and ethnic minorities in the U.S. earned 99.0 cents for every dollar white employees earned in comparable jobs [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70]. The company reported that 647,000 corporate and operations employees engaged with the Together at Amazon Community in 2025, which includes 2,300 chapters of Employee-Led Groups (ELGs) across multiple countries and regions [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_75]. However, no gender or racial/ethnic representation data is provided by job level (e.g., leadership, management, operational), geography (e.g., North America, EMEA, APAC), or disability/LGBTQ+ status — nor are targets for representation published [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_75]. The source contains no disclosure of representation gaps, root-cause analysis of pay variances by level or region, progress against prior-year diversity goals, or accountability mechanisms for closing residual pay gaps [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_71][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_70].

### Supplier Social Assessment  
Amazon’s Supply Chain Standards — available in 23 languages — apply to all suppliers of goods and services, including subcontractors and recruitment agents, and require adherence to applicable laws and human rights standards [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_84][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_83]. In 2025, Amazon conducted 3,081 supplier audits across its logistics, warehousing, and construction supply chain, including 1,579 audits focused on third-party labor, service, and not-for-resale goods providers [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_85]. Audit findings are categorized as high-, medium-, or low-severity; high-severity findings require corrective action plans and follow-up audits [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88]. However, the source does not disclose the total number or percentage of suppliers assessed, the number or rate of non-compliant suppliers, the proportion of high-risk findings unresolved after 90 days, or audit results disaggregated by tier (Tier 1–3) or geography [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_85]. No supplier non-compliance rate or remediation timeline metric is reported [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_88].

### Supporting a Just Climate Transition  
Amazon states it aims to integrate human rights due diligence into its decarbonization efforts “so we can better identify how our shift to a green economy might affect the communities in our value chain” [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66]. In 2025, it focused on carbon-free energy procurement, climate finance, and community-based carbon neutralization projects to align its net-zero commitment with human rights principles [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_67]. However, the source contains no TCFD-aligned social impact assessment of Amazon’s net-zero pathway — including no analysis of projected workforce transitions, reskilling needs, community displacement risks, or equity safeguards for affected workers or regions [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66]. No baseline, target year, or measurable indicator is provided for human rights integration into climate strategy [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_66].

### Not covered in source material

GRI 403-3: Science-aligned, time-bound occupational health & safety target (e.g., “RIR ≤ 2.0 by 2030”, with 2025 baseline).

GRI 404-2: Forward-looking target for training coverage or effectiveness (e.g., “100% of procurement staff trained on human rights by 2026”).  
GRI 405-2 and 405-3: Gender and racial/ethnic representation by job level (e.g., senior leadership, management, operational staff) and major region (e.g., North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific); disability and LGBTQ+ representation metrics.  
GRI 414-3 and 414-4: Number and percentage of suppliers assessed, non-compliant suppliers, and remediation status — disaggregated by tier (Tier 1–3), geography, and severity level; supplier non-compliance rate; % of high-risk findings unresolved after 90 days.

### GRI 2-11: Board Diversity Composition  
The source material states that the Board’s composition is evaluated for “diversity of experiences, backgrounds, and perspectives” and that recruitment considers “skills in the context of identifying and evaluating new director candidates” [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. However, no quantitative data on board diversity—including percentage of women directors, representation of underrepresented ethnicities, average director tenure, or comparative figures for 2024—is disclosed in the provided context [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102]. Therefore, metrics required by GRI 2-11 (e.g., “proportion of individuals appointed to the highest governance body who are women and members of under-represented groups”) cannot be reported [GRI 2-11].

### TCFD Governance A1: Board Climate Risk Oversight Evidence  
The Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee is explicitly responsible for overseeing climate-related risks as part of its mandate for sustainability and environmental risk management [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_103][TCFD Governance A1]. The Chief Sustainability Officer provides “regular updates” to this committee on sustainability performance, including climate-related matters [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104][TCFD Governance A1]. However, the source material does not specify the frequency (e.g., quarterly, biannual), format (e.g., written reports, presentations with scenario analysis), or analytical methodology (e.g., physical risk mapping, transition risk assessment) used in these climate risk updates [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104]. It also does not state whether climate risk is reviewed by the full Board or other committees beyond the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee [TCFD Governance A1]. No time-bound target for board-level climate risk integration (e.g., “full Board climate risk review implemented annually starting 2026”) is disclosed [TCFD Governance A1].

### GRI 205-1: Anti-Corruption and Ethics Performance Metrics  
Amazon operates a confidential, third-party-managed Ethics Line available in 65 countries and 165 languages, enabling anonymous reporting of Code violations and ethical concerns [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. The Business Conduct and Ethics team records, investigates, and tracks remediation of reported issues, with findings escalated to the Audit Committee [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. Senior leadership receives regular updates on harassment and discrimination allegations involving director-level personnel; the Leadership Development and Compensation Committee receives detailed quarterly updates for vice-president-level and above cases or those subject to external investigation [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][GRI 205-1]. However, the source material does not disclose the total number of Ethics Line reports received in 2025 or 2024, the number of substantiated corruption allegations, investigations opened or closed, disciplinary actions taken, average or median resolution time, or any instances where investigations exceeded 90-day resolution targets [GRI 205-1]. No 2024 baseline or year-on-year comparison is provided for any ethics performance metric [GRI 205-1].

### GRI 205-2: Anti-Corruption Targets  
The source material confirms Amazon’s internal policy prohibition on bribery “for any reason, whether in dealings with governments or the private sector” and notes participation in external anti-corruption initiatives such as the OECD’s Anti-Corruption Leaders Hub [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107][GRI 205-2]. However, no forward-looking, quantified, time-bound anti-corruption target—such as a reduction in substantiated ethics violations by a defined percentage from a stated baseline year—is disclosed [GRI 205-2]. No deadline, metric definition, or baseline year (e.g., “reduce substantiated corruption cases by 15% by 2027, from 2025 baseline”) appears in the context [GRI 205-2].

### Not covered in source material  
- GRI 2-11: Quantitative board diversity composition (e.g., % women, % underrepresented ethnicities, average director tenure) for 2024 and 2025 [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102].  
- TCFD Governance A1: Frequency, format, or analytical methodology (e.g., scenario analysis) of climate risk updates to the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee; evidence of climate risk review by the full Board or other committees; or a time-bound target for board-level climate risk integration (e.g., “annual full Board climate risk review adopted by end-2026”) [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_103][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_104].  
- GRI 205-1: Total Ethics Line reports, substantiated corruption allegations, investigations opened/closed, disciplinary actions taken, resolution timelines (including % exceeding 90 days), root-cause explanations for delays, or 2024–2025 comparative data [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107].  
- GRI 205-2: Forward-looking, quantified anti-corruption target (e.g., reduction in substantiated ethics violations) with defined baseline year, deadline, and metric [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_106][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107].  
- Jurisdictional limitations on political contribution reporting, supplier human rights assessment coverage rates, or definitions of “risk-based” in third-party due diligence [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_107].  
- Board and committee meeting frequencies for 2024 (to enable year-on-year comparison with 2025’s six Board meetings, four Nominating and Corporate Governance meetings, five Leadership Development and Compensation meetings, six Audit meetings, and two Security meetings) [2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_101][2025-amazon-sustainability-report_chunk_102].
